title: Social cognitive theory: An agentic perspective
finding: Defines human agency by intentionality, forethought, self-reactiveness and self-reflectiveness, in three modes: personal, proxy and collective; AI use fits proxy agency.
ai_use: yes (cited as the base definition in AI agency papers)

title: Toward a psychology of human agency
finding: Restates the four core properties of agency and the personal/proxy/collective modes.

title: What is agency?
finding: Splits agency into iterational (habit), projective (imagining futures) and practical-evaluative (judgement in the moment) elements.

title: Well-being, agency and freedom: The Dewey Lectures 1984
finding: Separates agency (pursuing goals one values) from wellbeing; basis of the capability approach used by Chooi, Lee & Li 2026.

title: Agency and empowerment: A proposal for internationally comparable indicators
finding: Proposes survey indicators of agency and empowerment (including relative autonomy and control over decisions) for household surveys.
longitudinal_use: used in repeated household surveys (not checked)

title: Future of Work with AI Agents: Auditing Automation and Augmentation Potential across the U.S. Workforce (Human Agency Scale)
finding: Human Agency Scale H1 (AI does task alone) to H5 (continuous human involvement essential); H3 equal partnership is the most-wanted level in 47 of 104 occupations.
limits: measures preferred involvement, not actual capacity

title: HumanAgencyBench: Scalable Evaluation of Human Agency Support in AI Assistants
finding: Scores assistants on six behaviours (ask clarifying questions, avoid value manipulation, correct misinformation, defer important decisions, encourage learning, maintain social boundaries); support is low to moderate and does not rise with capability.
limits: LLM-simulated users and LLM judges; no human outcomes

title: Who's in Charge? Disempowerment Patterns in Real-World LLM Usage
finding: Taxonomy of situational disempowerment potential (reality, value-judgement and action distortion) plus four amplifiers (authority projection, attachment, reliance & dependency, vulnerability); severe reality distortion is about 1 in 1,300 conversations.
limits: single provider; potential, not measured harm; authors overlap with Kulveit et al.
longitudinal_use: prevalence tracked over time in logs (not same people)

title: AI control items AICONTROL1/AICONTROL2 (American Trends Panel)
finding: How much control people think they have over whether AI is used in their life: 57% not too much or none (2025) vs 59% (2024); 61% want more control (55% in 2024).
longitudinal_use: asked twice (2024, 2025); not analysed as a panel

title: AI impact on human abilities items (HUMNIMPCT; AI2HAPPEN)
finding: 53% expect AI to make people worse at thinking creatively, 40% worse at difficult decisions, 50% worse at forming relationships; 51% extremely or very concerned that people's ability to do things on their own will get worse.
limits: beliefs about others, not measured skill

title: Political efficacy items ('allows people like you to have a say')
finding: Repeated items on whether the political system lets people like you have a say: a long-running baseline for perceived say, not tied to AI.

title: Internal and external political efficacy items
finding: Long-running items on whether people feel they understand politics and have a say in what government does.
longitudinal_use: repeated cross-sections; some ANES panel components

title: Measuring AI-Induced Disempowerment: A Framework and Proposed Metrics
finding: Three layers (exposure, erosion, lock-in) grounded in Sen; proposes six metrics: with/without-AI evaluations, disempowerment perception surveys tracked over 6 months to 3 years, AI content saturation, capital flows to labour, human-AI task frontier, institutional ethnography.

title: Gradual Disempowerment: Systemic Existential Risks from Incremental AI Development
finding: Argues AI replacing human labour and cognition weakens both explicit control and the implicit alignment of economy, culture and states, risking an effectively irreversible loss of human influence.

title: Human autonomy in the age of artificial intelligence
finding: Defines autonomy as effective capacity for self-governance with two dimensions: authenticity (values are one's own; threatened by manipulation) and agency (able to act on them; threatened by lost options and competence).

title: AI Systems and Respect for Human Autonomy
finding: Lists six aspects of autonomy: capacities, exercise, recognition by others, self-respect, normative requirements on others, and external resources.

title: Relational Autonomy: Feminist Perspectives on Autonomy, Agency, and the Social Self
finding: Holds that autonomy is built through social relations; contrasted with procedural and substantive accounts.

title: Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being
finding: Treats autonomy, competence and relatedness as basic needs; autonomy means behaviour experienced as self-endorsed.
ai_use: yes (SDT widely applied to AI at work and in education)

title: Basic Psychological Need Satisfaction and Frustration Scale (BPNSFS)
finding: 24 items measuring satisfaction and frustration of autonomy, competence and relatedness; 12-item diary version and domain forms (work form experimental).
ai_use: likely (SDT need measures in AI-at-work studies; examples not checked in this pass)

title: Index of Autonomous Functioning (IAF)
finding: Trait autonomy with three subscales: authorship/self-congruence, interest-taking, and low susceptibility to control.
limits: trait measure; interest-taking subscale still exploratory

title: Relative Autonomy Index (self-regulation questionnaires)
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
finding: Weights external, introjected, identified and intrinsic reasons into one score of how self-determined a behaviour is.
ai_use: could be adapted to reasons for using AI (none found in this search)
longitudinal_use: widely used in repeated designs outside AI

title: Supporting human autonomy in AI systems: A framework for ethical enquiry
finding: Applies SDT to AI design and separates the spheres where autonomy can be supported or undermined, from adopting a technology through to life and society.

cite: Santoni de Sio & van den Hoven 2018
title: Meaningful human control over autonomous systems: A philosophical account
finding: Meaningful human control requires 'tracking' (system responds to human reasons) and 'tracing' (outcomes traceable to a human who understands them).

title: A five-stage model of the mental activities involved in directed skill acquisition
finding: Novice, advanced beginner, competent, proficient, expert: moving from rules to intuitive, situation-based performance.

title: The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance
finding: Expert performance reflects long, effortful, feedback-rich deliberate practice, which implies that taking away practice opportunities threatens expertise.
limits: magnitude of practice effect disputed by later meta-analyses

title: The third wave of science studies: Studies of expertise and experience
finding: Distinguishes contributory expertise (can do the work) from interactional expertise (can talk the domain's language).

title: Factors that influence skill decay and retention: A quantitative review and analysis
finding: Meta-analysis showing skill decays with longer non-use intervals, with task type and conditions shaping how fast.
limits: pre-AI; effect sizes not re-checked here

title: The retention of manual flying skills in the automated cockpit
finding: Hand-flying and instrument scanning were mostly intact, but cognitive skills (tracking position, choosing the next navigation step, spotting failures) degraded, linked to mind-wandering under automation.

title: From here to autonomy: Lessons learned from human-automation research
finding: Describes an 'automation conundrum': as automation becomes more capable and reliable, operators' situation awareness falls and taking over becomes harder.

title: Ironies of automation
finding: Automation leaves humans the hardest tasks (monitoring, rare takeovers) while removing the practice those tasks need.

title: Labor and Monopoly Capital: The Degradation of Work in the Twentieth Century
finding: Deskilling thesis: management splits planning from doing and uses technology to reduce the skill content of jobs.

title: How much automation is too much? Keeping the human relevant in knowledge work
venue: Journal of Emerging Technologies in Accounting
finding: Argues that intelligent automation in accounting can deskill professionals (the 'deskilling paradox'), threatening the judgement it relies on.
limits: page could not be fetched this session; details from memory

title: The vicious circles of skill erosion: A case study of cognitive automation
venue: Journal of the Association for Information Systems
finding: Case study describing self-reinforcing loops in which automation erodes staff skills and awareness, making the organisation more reliant on the system.

title: Does using artificial intelligence assistance accelerate skill decay and hinder skill development without performers' awareness?
finding: Argues AI assistance may speed skill decay and block skill development while users do not notice.
limits: page redirected and not read; title from memory

title: Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC)
finding: Measures adults' proficiency in literacy, numeracy and problem solving; usable as an unaided-skill population baseline.
limits: cross-sectional cycles about a decade apart; no AI-use linkage
ai_use: indirect (baseline only; no AI items checked)

title: A behavioral model of rational choice
finding: Bounded rationality: people satisfice under limited information, time and computation.

title: Dual-process theories of higher cognition: Advancing the debate
finding: Type 1 (fast, autonomous) vs Type 2 (working-memory-dependent, reflective) processing.
ai_use: yes (used to frame cognitive forcing and AI over-reliance)

title: A model for types and levels of human interaction with automation
venue: IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics A
finding: Four stages (information acquisition, analysis, decision selection, action implementation), each automatable to a different level.
ai_use: yes (used to classify AI decision support)

title: Adult Decision-Making Competence (A-DMC)
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
finding: Behavioural battery of decision skills (e.g., resistance to framing, consistency in risk perception, applying decision rules).

title: General Decision-Making Style (GDMS)
finding: Five decision styles: rational, intuitive, dependent (relying on others' advice), avoidant, spontaneous; the dependent subscale is a candidate baseline for AI dependence.

title: Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT)
finding: Three items where an intuitive wrong answer must be overridden; a short measure of reflective thinking.
limits: item familiarity; answers now easy to look up with AI

title: Decisional Conflict Scale
finding: Measures uncertainty, feeling informed, values clarity and support in health decisions.

cite: Judge-advisor system paradigm (e.g., Bonaccio & Dalal 2006 review)
title: Weight of advice (WOA) / advice-taking paradigm
venue: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
finding: Person gives an initial estimate, sees advice, then revises; WOA = share of the gap moved toward the advice.
ai_use: yes (core paradigm in algorithm appreciation and aversion work)

title: Algorithm aversion: People erroneously avoid algorithms after seeing them err
finding: People abandon an algorithm after seeing it err, even when it beats humans (under-reliance).

title: Algorithm appreciation: People prefer algorithmic to human judgment
venue: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
finding: Lay people weight algorithmic advice more than human advice in many estimation tasks (counterpoint to aversion).

title: Agreement fraction and switch fraction (reliance metrics)
finding: Behavioural reliance metrics: how often final answers agree with the model and how often people switch to it after disagreeing.

title: Appropriate Reliance on AI Advice: Conceptualization and the Effect of Explanations (AoR: RAIR and RSR)
finding: Appropriateness of reliance as two ratios: RAIR (switching to correct AI advice when initially wrong) and RSR (keeping a correct answer against wrong AI advice).
limits: needs ground truth and an initial unaided answer

title: Automation bias commission and omission errors
finding: Measures automation bias as commission errors (following wrong prompts) and omission errors (missing events the aid did not flag).

title: Critical Thinking: A Statement of Expert Consensus (Delphi Report)
finding: Defines critical thinking as purposeful, self-regulatory judgement and lists core skills and dispositions; basis of the CCTDI.

title: California Critical Thinking Disposition Inventory (CCTDI)
finding: Commercial inventory of critical-thinking dispositions (e.g., truth-seeking, open-mindedness, analyticity).

title: Critical Thinking Disposition Scale (CTDS)
finding: Short free disposition scale with two factors: critical openness and reflective scepticism.

title: Halpern Critical Thinking Assessment (HCTA)
finding: Performance test of critical thinking with open and forced-choice items across everyday scenarios.

title: Need for Cognition Scale (NCS-18)
finding: 18-item measure of the tendency to engage in and enjoy effortful thinking.
ai_use: yes (moderator of AI over-reliance in cognitive-forcing studies)
longitudinal_use: trait; rarely tracked over AI exposure

title: Metacognitive Awareness Inventory (MAI)
finding: 52 items on knowledge of cognition and regulation of cognition.

title: Metacognitive efficiency (meta-d') and calibration measures
finding: Signal-detection measure of how well confidence tracks accuracy, independent of performance level.
ai_use: yes (confidence-accuracy measures in AI-assisted reasoning studies)

title: The Metacognitive Demands and Opportunities of Generative AI
finding: Argues GenAI imposes metacognitive demands (monitoring and control while prompting, judging outputs, and planning workflows) and proposes design support.

title: The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking: Self-Reported Reductions in Cognitive Effort and Confidence Effects From a Survey of Knowledge Workers
finding: Study-specific measure of perceived critical-thinking enactment and effort per task; confidence in GenAI predicts less critical thinking, self-confidence more.

title: AI Tools in Society: Impacts on Cognitive Offloading and the Future of Critical Thinking (questionnaire)
finding: 23-item critical-thinking questionnaire drawing on HCTA plus self-reported AI use and offloading; AI use correlates r = -0.68 with critical thinking and +0.72 with offloading.
limits: cross-sectional; scoring unclear; mediation language on correlational data

title: Performance and Metacognition Disconnect when Reasoning in Human-AI Interaction
finding: Pairs LSAT performance with self-estimated scores; AI users improved but overestimated by about 4 points and the Dunning-Kruger pattern disappeared; higher AI literacy linked to worse self-assessment.

title: Trust in automation: Designing for appropriate reliance
finding: Integrative review: trust guides reliance on automation when complexity makes full understanding impractical; proposes a model of trust dynamics, context and display.

title: Humans and automation: Use, misuse, disuse, abuse
finding: Four patterns: use (voluntary engagement), misuse (over-reliance), disuse (neglect, often after false alarms), abuse (automating without regard to human performance).

title: Trust between People and Automation scale (Checklist for Trust; 'Jian scale')
finding: 12-item trust-in-automation questionnaire spanning distrust and trust; the most reused trust scale in automation and AI studies.
limits: factor structure debated (one vs two factors); not re-checked at source
longitudinal_use: repeated within sessions common; multi-week rare

title: Trust in Automation questionnaire (TiA)
venue: Proceedings of the IEA Congress (Springer AISC)
finding: Subscales including reliability/competence, understanding/predictability, familiarity, intention of developers, propensity to trust, and trust in automation.
limits: built for automated driving; not re-checked

title: Measures for explainable AI (incl. 8-item XAI Trust Scale)
finding: Proposes measures of explanation goodness, satisfaction, mental models, curiosity, trust (8 items mostly from the Cahour-Fourzy scale) and human-AI performance.

title: Complacency-Potential Rating Scale (CPRS)
finding: 16 items, four factors (confidence, reliance, trust, safety) on attitudes predicting automation complacency.
limits: factor structure did not replicate in Merritt et al. 2019

title: Automation-Induced Complacency Potential-Revised (AICP-R)
finding: 10 items, two weakly related factors (alleviating workload; monitoring); only Monitoring predicted hypothetical complacency.

title: Cognitive offloading
finding: Defines offloading as using physical action to reduce a task's cognitive demand; offloading depends on effort and on metacognitive beliefs about one's ability, which can be inaccurate.

title: The extended mind
finding: Counter-view: reliably available, trusted external resources can be part of a person's cognitive system, so reliance need not mean loss.

title: Epistemic dependence
finding: Argues that rationally relying on experts one cannot check is a normal part of knowledge, so dependence is not irrational in itself.

title: Are we overpathologizing everyday life? A tenable blueprint for behavioral addiction research
finding: Critique of copying addiction criteria onto new everyday behaviours without evidence of harm; relevant to 'AI addiction' scales.
ai_use: relevant critique (not checked for AI citations)

title: Scale for Dependence on Artificial Intelligence (DIA)
finding: 5 items, one factor (alpha 0.87); invariant by gender.

title: Generative AI Dependency Scale
finding: Three factors (cognitive preoccupation, negative consequences, withdrawal) under a higher-order dependency factor; invariant across sex and US/Singapore.

title: Problematic ChatGPT Use Scale (PCGUS), Turkish adaptation
venue: International Journal of Mental Health and Addiction
finding: 9 items (from an 11-item original), one factor, alpha about 0.88-0.90.

title: Which Economic Tasks are Performed with AI? Evidence from Millions of Claude Conversations (automation vs augmentation)
finding: Classifies usage as augmentation (e.g., learning, iterating) or automation (minimal human involvement); 57% augmentation, 43% automation.

title: Self-efficacy: Toward a unifying theory of behavioral change
finding: Self-efficacy is belief in one's ability to execute the actions a goal requires; built from mastery, vicarious experience, persuasion and physiological states.

title: General Self-Efficacy Scale (GSE)
finding: 10-item general self-efficacy scale, translated into many languages.
ai_use: yes (covariate in AI studies; examples not checked)
longitudinal_use: widely used in panels outside AI

title: Computer Self-Efficacy measure
finding: 10-item measure of confidence in using a new software package under varying support; template for AI self-efficacy items.

title: Artificial Intelligence Self-Efficacy Scale (AISES)
finding: Self-efficacy for using AI; reported factors include assistance, anthropomorphic interaction, comfort with AI and technological skills (not checked at source).
limits: page rate-limited this session; measures efficacy with AI, not without it

title: MAILS - Meta AI Literacy Scale
venue: Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans
finding: AI literacy questionnaire that adds psychological meta-competencies (AI self-efficacy and self-competency) to knowledge and use dimensions.
longitudinal_use: pre/post in some course evaluations (not checked)

title: Scale for the assessment of non-experts' AI literacy (SNAIL)
finding: Self-assessed AI literacy with factors for technical understanding, critical appraisal and practical application (not checked at source).

title: AI Literacy Scale (AILS)
finding: 12 items across awareness, usage, evaluation and ethics (not checked at source).

title: Beyond the comparator model: A multifactorial two-step account of agency
finding: Separates a non-conceptual feeling of agency (weighted cues) from a conceptual judgement of agency (explicit attribution).

title: Intentional binding paradigm
finding: Implicit measure: voluntary actions and their outcomes are perceived as closer in time; involuntary movements reverse the effect.
ai_use: yes (automation and human-agent studies, e.g., Berberian et al. 2012; not re-checked)

title: Sense of Agency Scale (SoAS)
finding: 11 items, two factors (positive and negative sense of agency); 2-month test-retest r = 0.74-0.78; related to but distinct from self-efficacy and locus of control.

title: Sense of Agency Rating Scale (SOARS)
finding: State measure of altered agency (involuntariness and effortlessness) after a task.

title: The experience of agency in human-computer interactions: A review
finding: Reviews how interface design affects users' sense of agency and argues for implicit measures such as intentional binding in HCI.

title: Psychological ownership scale
finding: Short scale of feeling that a target (job, organisation, product) is 'mine'; adapted for ownership of AI-assisted text.
ai_use: yes (adapted in AI co-writing studies; not re-checked)

title: Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task (EEG + ownership + recall battery)
finding: Combines EEG connectivity, essay ownership and ability to quote one's own essay; LLM users had weakest connectivity and lowest ownership, and LLM-to-brain switchers showed under-engagement in session 4.

title: General Attitudes towards Artificial Intelligence Scale (GAAIS)
finding: Positive and negative attitude subscales toward AI; confirmatory validation followed in 2023 (details not re-checked).

title: ATTARI-12 (Attitudes Towards Artificial Intelligence)
finding: 12 items covering cognitive, affective and behavioural components; essentially one factor; 31-day test-retest r = 0.80.

title: AI Attitude Scale (AIAS-4)
finding: 4-item, one-factor brief measure of general attitude toward AI on a 10-point scale.

title: Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale (AIAS)
finding: Four factors: learning, job replacement, sociotechnical blindness and AI configuration (not checked at source).

title: UTAUT2 (acceptance and use of technology)
finding: Predicts intention and use from performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, hedonic motivation, price value and habit.
ai_use: yes (dominant model in GenAI adoption surveys)

cite: Gillespie et al. (University of Melbourne & KPMG)
title: Trust, attitudes and use of AI: global study
finding: Cross-national survey of trust in AI, AI use and attitudes, repeated across editions.

title: Competing technologies, increasing returns, and lock-in by historical events
finding: Increasing returns can lock a market into one technology through small early events, making later switching costly.

title: Clio and the economics of QWERTY
finding: Path dependence: technical interrelatedness, scale economies and quasi-irreversible investments (including skills) keep inferior standards in place.

title: Measurement of situation awareness in dynamic systems (incl. SAGAT freeze-probe method)
finding: Measures situation awareness by freezing a simulation and querying operators; standard tool for out-of-the-loop effects.
limits: needs simulation; not used with LLMs (none found in this search)

title: NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX)
finding: Six workload subscales: mental, physical and temporal demand, performance, effort, frustration.
limits: lower workload is not the same as less learning
